newsitem.title: USA: Gourmet coffee drinkers may soon see a price hike.
newsitem.headline: Gourmet coffee drinkers may soon see a price hike.

text.p: Coffee aficionados who buy pricey gourmet beans like Sumatra Mandhelings and Ethiopian Yirgacheffes may soon pay even more due to the surge in coffee futures, speciality roasters say.

Futures prices for coffee have nearly doubled since the beginning of the year amid low inventory levels in consuming countries, labour unrest in top producers Brazil and Colombia and concerns about Latin American supply.

While some roasters of high-quality beans attending the Speciality Coffee Association of America's conference have held off on a retail price hike, most processers said they have already passed on higher costs to the consumer -- and are considering another price increase.
"We recently raised our prices 40 cents (per pound)," one Columbus, Ohio-based retailer and roaster said. "And we're looking for another 40-cent increase in the next month-and-a-half."
The roaster said U.S. processors' "just-in-time" inventory management have given them less purchasing flexibility and forced them to pay up for sorely needed beans.
Another roaster agreed. "The smaller roaster buys order-to-order and has to pay the prevailing market rate," he said. "If the market keeps going up they have to raise prices."

Additionally, the speciality coffee market has experienced strong growth, causing a supply squeeze on high-quality mild coffees. Gourmet coffee outlets have soared from about 200 in 1989 to over 5,000, and the Speciality Coffee Association estimates outlets will double to 10,000 in 1999.
"The industry craze is finally starting to have an effect on supply," said one Washington, D.C.-based roaster. "From what we're hearing it could be worse in six months."

Industry analysts expect the tight supply situation to spill over into the next half of the year. The key, they said, is the upcoming 1997/98 harvest in top-grower Brazil which is forecast to come in below the current crop year.
Still, some roasters hesitate to hike prices because they fear it will anger customers and hurt consumption.

"We don't want to scare them off. They may end up buying a lower quality product," said one New Orleans-based roaster. "There's got to be some ceiling price where consumers say 'enough is enough,'" he added.
But other speciality industry participants said gourmet coffee drinkers, who are used to paying top-dollar for exotic beans, will eventually accept a price increase.

"If we do it correctly and tell our story, the consumer will understand," said Speciality Coffee Association Executive Director Ted Lingle. "It may have a short-term impact, but even at $15 a pound they still want to make it a part of their life.
"What we have found in the past is that consumers not only decided they wanted it, but they want quality for what they are paying for."
